newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian fuel crunch seen easing by weekend.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian fuel crunch seen easing by weekend.

text.p: An acute fuel shortage in Nigeria, Africa's leading oil-producing nation, should abate by Friday, oil ministry officials said on Tuesday.
The military rulers ended an emergency meeting in the capital Abuja on Monday night pledging to end the five-week-old crisis within 48 hours.
Although Nigeria frequently experiences fuel shortage the current crunch has been the most serious since a 1994 strike by oil workers.
It has caused serious hardship for thousands of commuters, many of whom had to trek to work. Many businesses have closed temporarily.
Motorists in Lagos welcomed the government's promise of early action and said more filling stations appeared to have fuel on Tuesday.
"There are a few more stations with fuel today but the queues are still long," said bus driver Okechukwu Okeke, adding "We hope the government will keep to its word because we have suffered enough."

A senior aide of oil minister Dan Etete said that the minister, before leaving Lagos on Monday for an Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) meeting in Vienna, had made a series of arrangements to rectify the situation.
"We are bringing the situation under control and by Friday there should be fuel everywhere," he said.
He declined to give the source of fuel being sold in Lagos on Tuesday. Throughout the weekend filling stations in the sprawling metropolis were dry.

At the end of their Abuja meeting, Kano state military administrator Colonel Dominic Oneya told reporters that the military ruler General Sani Abacha had ordered that fuel should be made available through imports while efforts would be made to get Nigeria's epileptic refineries to go into full production.
Allowing imports is a major climbdown by Abacha, who stopped fuel imports in September last year and ordered state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation to get local refineries to work.
Nigeria produces about two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and exports all of its production, except for 250,000 bpd allocated to its four refineries for processing into fuel products.

No exact reason has been given for the current shortage but it is no secret that the refineries have long been operating at a fraction of their 445,000 bpd installed capacity because of lack of maintenance and mismanagement.
The head of the manufacturing association warned of an imminent collapse of industries if the situation was not checked, labelling it "a national shame".
The black market cashed in on the shortage with touts charging several times the official pump price.

In Abacha's home state Kano, youths staged a peaceful protest on Monday to demand an immediate normalisation of the situation. University students warned of public protests if the situation was not redressed.
